stories.headline: The euro sinks to a 17-month low as France’s debt and Spain’s snap election spook investors
stories.dek: Money traders fear Europe’s debt troubles could spread from Paris to the rest of the eurozone.
stories.caveman: The euro is the money used by 20 European countries. On Monday (Oct. 5) it fell to its weakest level against the U.S. dollar since May 2025 — about $1.116 at the low point — before bouncing back a little to around $1.12. Two things scared traders. First, France: its government owes a lot of money (debt is expected to reach almost 122% of the whole economy next year), and its new 2027 budget only cuts the yearly deficit a little, from 5.4% to 5% of GDP. The interest France pays on 10-year loans hit about 4.8%, the highest since the 2011 euro crisis. Second, Spain: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez suddenly called an early election for Nov. 29. Simple: when investors worry about a country’s politics and debt, they sell its money.
stories.why_it_matters: A weaker euro makes oil and other imports (priced in dollars) more expensive for Europeans, at a time when eurozone inflation is already 3.8%. It also puts the European Central Bank in a tight spot: raise rates to fight prices, or hold off so debt-heavy countries like France don’t crack.
stories.camps: Some analysts warn this looks like the start of a new eurozone debt scare, with France as the “poster child” and its far-right, big-spending candidates gaining ahead of the April 2027 presidential vote. Others say the panic is overdone: the euro recovered more than half its drop the same day, France’s government insists it is a reliable borrower, and Europe’s central bank has tools to calm markets if needed.
stories.image_alt: The Paris skyline with the Eiffel Tower in a hazy sky

terms.explain: The shared currency (money) of 20 European Union countries, including France, Germany and Spain.
When a government spends more in a year than it collects in taxes, the gap is the deficit. It borrows to fill it.
Gross domestic product: the total value of everything a country makes and sells in a year. Used to measure how big debts are.
An election called earlier than planned, often to break a deadlock.
The central bank for the euro. It sets interest rates for all countries that use the euro.

stories.headline: Nasdaq hits a record even as a key U.S. borrowing rate climbs to its highest since 2002
stories.dek: Big buyouts and AI excitement lift stocks, while the 10-year Treasury yield reaches 5.31%.
stories.caveman: On Monday (Oct. 5) U.S. stocks went up. The S&P 500 rose 0.7% to 7,773.95 — just 0.3% below its all-time high. The tech-heavy Nasdaq rose 1.1% to a new record. Two company buyouts helped: a French firm agreed to buy software maker PTC (its stock jumped 33.5%), and C.H. Robinson agreed to buy trucking broker RXO (up 22.5%). Nvidia, the AI chip giant, rose 2.1%. But at the same time, the interest rate on 10-year U.S. government bonds rose to 5.31%, the highest close since April 2002. Brent crude oil swung between $100 and $103 a barrel before ending near $100. Simple: stock buyers are cheerful about AI, while bond buyers are demanding more money to lend to the government.
stories.why_it_matters: The 10-year Treasury rate guides what Americans pay on mortgages, car loans and business loans. When it climbs this high, buying a home gets more expensive — even while the stock market looks great for people who own shares.
stories.camps: Optimists say strong company profits, solid consumer spending and the AI building boom can keep stocks rising even with higher rates. Skeptics point out that only a narrow group of big tech stocks is doing most of the lifting, that high oil prices from the Iran war keep inflation risk alive, and that rates this high have ended rallies before.
stories.image_alt: The carved front of the New York Stock Exchange building

terms.explain: A list of about 500 big U.S. companies. Its up-and-down is the most common way to measure the stock market.
A U.S. stock market index full of technology companies.
The interest rate the U.S. government pays when it borrows by selling bonds. Higher yield = borrowing costs more.
When one company buys another company, usually by paying cash for its shares.
A type of crude oil whose price is used as the main world benchmark.

stories.headline: France’s Schneider Electric will buy U.S. software maker PTC for $22.6 billion
stories.dek: The all-cash deal is a big bet that factories will soon run on artificial intelligence.
stories.caveman: Schneider Electric is a giant French company that makes equipment to control electricity in buildings, factories and data centers. On Monday (Oct. 5) it agreed to buy PTC, a Boston company whose software helps engineers design products and run factories. Schneider will pay $205 cash for every PTC share — a 42% premium over the stock’s price the day before. That values PTC at about $22.6 billion. To pay for it, Schneider will borrow about €16–17 billion and sell about €5–6 billion in new shares. PTC’s board supports the deal. It still needs a vote by PTC owners and government approvals, including a U.S. national-security review, and should close by late 2027. PTC stock jumped 33.5%; Schneider’s stock fell about 10% in Paris.
stories.why_it_matters: It is one of the biggest bets yet that “industrial AI” — smart software that designs and runs factories and power systems — will be a huge business. It also shows European companies buying American tech know-how.
stories.camps: Supporters say combining power equipment with design software gives customers one connected system and could create billions in new sales. Doubters, including some Schneider investors who sold the stock, say the price is very high, the debt is large, and big mergers often promise more savings than they deliver. U.S. regulators may also look closely at a foreign buyer of important industrial software.
stories.image_alt: The Schneider Electric logo on a green background

terms.explain: Extra money paid above a stock’s current price to convince owners to sell.
A purchase paid fully with money, not with the buyer’s own shares.
Artificial intelligence used in factories, power grids and machines, not just chatbots.
A U.S. government committee that checks whether foreign purchases of American companies could hurt national security.
The group of people chosen to oversee a company and protect its owners’ interests.

stories.headline: Iran’s money hits a record low as its oil sales dry up under a U.S. blockade
stories.dek: Tehran insists it still controls the Strait of Hormuz; its oil minister resigns.
stories.caveman: The U.S. and Israel have been at war with Iran since early this year. The U.S. is blocking Iran’s oil sales, and Iran is keeping the Strait of Hormuz — a narrow sea lane where much of the world’s oil passes — mostly closed. On Monday (Oct. 5) Iran’s money, the rial, fell to a record low: on the street market one U.S. dollar now costs about 270,000 tomans, double what it cost in January. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Iran did not load a single barrel of oil onto tankers in September. Iran’s oil minister resigned, officially for “family reasons.” Iran’s military said it still controls every ship movement in Hormuz. Its foreign minister said the strait could reopen within seven days if Iran’s conditions are met. Ships keep getting attacked — at least one attack a day since Oct. 2.
stories.why_it_matters: For ordinary Iranians, a collapsing currency means food and medicine prices shoot up. For the world, Hormuz is a key reason oil sits near $100 a barrel, which pushes up gas and shipping prices everywhere.
stories.camps: The Trump administration says squeezing Iran’s oil money is working and will force Tehran to make a deal. Iran’s leaders say they will not accept “one-sided demands” and that only fair talks can end the war. Humanitarian groups warn that ordinary Iranians, not leaders, feel the pain of sanctions first. Meanwhile, other Gulf countries have found new routes and now ship more oil than before the war.
stories.image_alt: Iranian missiles on display in front of a large portrait in Tehran

terms.explain: Iran’s official money. People often count in tomans; one toman = 10 rials.
A narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman. A large share of the world’s oil tankers normally sail through it.
Using ships or force to stop goods from going in or out of a place.
Penalties, like trade bans, that countries use to pressure another government.

stories.headline: Under oath at NYC City Hall, AI giants can’t say how big the risk of disaster is
stories.dek: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta testify; Musk’s SpaceXAI skips a subpoena and faces a court fight.
stories.caveman: On Monday (Oct. 5) the New York City Council held a rare hearing on the dangers of artificial intelligence. Leaders from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta answered questions under oath, appearing by video link. Council Speaker Julie Menin asked: can any of you measure the chance of something catastrophic happening? None could. She called their answers “troubling at best.” Former AI researchers also spoke. Jacob Coxon, a whistleblower who quit Anthropic a few weeks ago warning that labs are “gambling with our lives,” said it is “more likely than not” that humans lose control of AI. Ex-Google DeepMind researcher Alex Turner said badly-behaved AI could become a bigger enemy than China. Elon Musk’s company SpaceXAI ignored a subpoena to appear; the council says it will go to court.
stories.why_it_matters: Washington has mostly let AI companies police themselves — President Trump signed a voluntary deal with tech leaders last week. Cities and states are now stepping in. What New York does could become a model (or a target) for other places.
stories.camps: Menin and safety researchers say AI that can “escape” or act on its own is too risky to leave to companies, and want local laws and legal liability. The companies say they take safety seriously and prefer one national rulebook; Google’s representative said “if it’s illegal without AI, it’s still illegal with AI.” Critics of city action argue a patchwork of local rules could slow U.S. innovation in the race with China.
stories.image_alt: NYC Council Speaker Julie Menin speaks at the AI hearing in the City Council chamber

terms.explain: Having promised to tell the truth; lying could be a crime (perjury).
A legal order that forces a person or company to testify or hand over documents.
The lawmaking body of a city. In New York, it has 51 members and is led by a Speaker.
AI that pursues goals its makers did not intend, possibly in harmful ways.
An insider who goes public about wrongdoing or danger inside an organization.

stories.headline: ChatGPT will start showing picture ads next to the images it makes
stories.dek: OpenAI expands advertising in the U.S. this month to pay for free and cheap plans.
stories.caveman: ChatGPT can draw pictures when you ask. Later this month, for U.S. users, OpenAI will start placing visual ads — pictures from advertisers — next to those generated images. Only a small test group of advertisers will be included at first. OpenAI says the ads will be clearly labeled and will not change ChatGPT’s answers. OpenAI first added ads earlier this year for free and low-cost users and expanded them to India in August. It is also adding tools that help advertisers track whether ads worked. ChatGPT has about 1.2 billion users every week. Simple: like Google and Facebook before it, the AI chatbot is becoming an ad business.
stories.why_it_matters: Ads shape what products get built. When a chatbot earns money from ads, people worry about whether it will quietly push them toward buying things — and how much of their personal chats are used to target them.
stories.camps: OpenAI says ads keep ChatGPT free for people who can’t pay, and promises that ads won’t influence answers. Privacy and consumer advocates worry that a chatbot knows far more about you than a search engine does, making ad targeting more powerful and ads harder to spot. Some observers say ads may also be a nudge to get casual users to pay for an ad-free subscription.
stories.image_alt: Two phone screens showing sample ChatGPT ads for grocery delivery

terms.explain: Ads made of pictures or graphics, like banners, rather than just text.
Choosing which ads to show you based on what a company knows about you.
Paying a regular fee (often monthly) for a service.
Pictures created by AI from a text request, not taken by a camera.

stories.headline: Kids learned the hard way about social media. Can America move faster on AI?
stories.dek: Parents and experts say chatbots, AI toys and homework bots need guardrails now, not years later.
stories.caveman: It took many years for the U.S. to seriously push back on the harms social media can do to kids. This summer, Meta agreed to an $18 billion settlement with states and promised new safety changes. Now kids are using something even more powerful: AI chatbots. According to Pew, 64% of U.S. teens have used them — mostly for schoolwork, but about 12% for emotional support or advice. Some kids form unhealthy bonds with chatbots, and companies sell AI toys for children as young as 2. AI companies are moving a bit faster than social media did: OpenAI added teen accounts in August that ban romantic chats. But Congress has passed no AI child-safety law; states are moving faster.
stories.why_it_matters: Children’s brains are still growing. Choices made now — about age checks, chatbot “relationships,” and AI toys — will shape a whole generation, the way phones and Instagram shaped the last one.
stories.camps: Advocates like parent Kristin Bride and psychologist Jonathan Haidt say: act early, don’t repeat the “oops” of social media. Tech companies point to new teen protections and say AI also helps kids learn. Some experts warn it’s harder to limit AI than social media, because kids use it for real homework help. The Trump administration has argued that too many state rules could slow U.S. AI companies.
stories.image_alt: A teenager’s ChatGPT history on a laptop screen at a coffee shop in Arkansas

terms.explain: An agreement to end a lawsuit, usually by paying money or promising changes, without a full trial.
A computer program you can talk or type with, like ChatGPT.
Ways for a website or app to check how old a user is.
A nonpartisan U.S. group that runs surveys about how people live and think.

stories.headline: She used Claude as a diary. Anthropic reported one entry to police — and she was arrested
stories.dek: A Florida woman faces a felony after an AI company flagged a chat threatening to “shoot up” a sheriff’s office.
stories.caveman: A woman in Lee County, Florida, typed messages to Anthropic’s AI chatbot, Claude. She later said she used it like a diary. On Sept. 26 she wrote that she would “shoot up” the local sheriff’s office; the next day she mentioned a new gun. Anthropic’s computers scan chats for dangerous phrases. Serious ones go to human reviewers. They reported this one to police; Anthropic’s privacy policy allows sharing with police to prevent serious harm. She was arrested at home without trouble and charged on Sept. 30 with a felony: a written or electronic threat of a mass shooting. It is at least the third Claude conversation to reach police since August. OpenAI has reported ChatGPT users too. Her court date is Nov. 2.
stories.why_it_matters: Many people tell chatbots things they would not tell a friend. This case shows those chats are not secret: companies read flagged ones and can send them to police. It raises big questions about privacy, safety and free speech.
stories.camps: Safety advocates and police say reporting real threats can prevent shootings, and that AI companies have been sued for NOT warning police in other cases. Privacy and civil-liberties voices worry about companies scanning private thoughts, about people venting with no real plan, and about who decides what counts as a threat. The sheriff’s message to users: what you tell an AI is “never truly anonymous.”
stories.image_alt: Anthropic’s Claude artwork: a line drawing of a face and connected dots on an orange background

terms.explain: A serious crime that can bring more than a year in prison.
When real people, not just software, look at flagged content to decide what to do.
A company’s written rules about what it does with your data, including when it shares it with police.
Basic freedoms protected from government overreach, such as free speech and privacy.

stories.headline: Spain’s Sánchez calls a surprise Nov. 29 election, betting on anger over housing
stories.dek: After the right-wing opposition blocked his emergency housing rules, the Socialist leader asks voters to decide.
stories.caveman: Pedro Sánchez is Spain’s prime minister. He leads a left-wing minority coalition government, which means he needs other parties’ votes to pass laws. Last month, Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman, was evicted from the Madrid home she had lived in for 70 years. Huge protests followed. Sánchez’s government wrote emergency housing rules — protection from eviction and automatic lease renewals. But on Friday (Oct. 2) the conservative People’s Party (PP), the far-right Vox and the Catalan party Junts voted them down. On Monday (Oct. 5) Sánchez called an early national election for Nov. 29 — Spain’s fifth in 10 years. Polls show the PP ahead, but probably needing Vox to govern.
stories.why_it_matters: If PP and Vox form a government together, it would be the first time a far-right party has helped rule Spain since dictator Francisco Franco died in 1975. Housing costs — a problem in many countries — are now the center of a national vote.
stories.camps: Sánchez frames it as a choice between joining a “far-right wave” or keeping Spain open and fair. The PP says eight years of Sánchez have not fixed housing, and points to corruption scandals around his party and inner circle and his failure to pass a budget since 2023. Vox pushes a “national priority” policy putting Spanish-born people first for housing. Some voters are simply tired of constant elections.
stories.image_alt: People in a café in Ronda, Spain, watch Pedro Sánchez on a TV screen
stories.image_credit: Photo: Jon Nazca/Reuters via The Guardian

terms.explain: A government whose party (or coalition) has less than half the seats, so it must win votes from others.
Forcing someone to leave their home, usually by a landlord with a court order.
Political groups on the extreme right, often strongly anti-immigration and nationalist.
Two or more parties joining together to govern.
A far-right Spanish party founded in 2013.

stories.headline: Saudi-backed forces launch “Yemen Dawn,” retaking towns near a key Red Sea chokepoint
stories.dek: With 100 fighter jets and U.S. intelligence help, Yemen’s government strikes back at the Iran-backed Houthis.
stories.caveman: Yemen has had a civil war since 2014. On one side: the Houthis, a rebel group backed by Iran, who hold the capital, Sanaa. On the other: Yemen’s internationally recognized government, backed by Saudi Arabia. A four-year ceasefire broke down this summer. In September the Houthis grabbed the coast along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, where about 12% of world trade passes. On Monday (Oct. 5) the government and a Saudi-led coalition launched a big offensive called “Yemen Dawn,” with 100 fighter jets. Officials say they retook the town of Dhubab and two others near the strait. A U.S. official said the U.S. helped with intelligence and planning. The Houthis had just captured Turbah, a key town near the city of Taiz.
stories.why_it_matters: This flare-up has killed at least 959 people and forced about 174,000 from their homes. Control of Bab el-Mandeb affects shipping and oil prices worldwide, on top of the Iran war’s closure of Hormuz.
stories.camps: Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government say they are defending themselves from Houthi missiles and want to “liberate” Sanaa; U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said they “have a right to defend themselves.” The Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of starting this round in July by bombing Sanaa’s airport, and have answered with missiles, drones and a blockade on Saudi-linked ships. U.N. agencies and health officials warn that a full return to war could deepen one of the world’s worst humanitarian disasters — the war has already killed more than 150,000 people.
stories.image_alt: A displaced man carries a gas cylinder through a tent camp near Aden, Yemen

terms.explain: A rebel movement from northern Yemen, backed by Iran, that controls the capital Sanaa and much of the north.
A narrow sea passage between Yemen and Africa that connects the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
A narrow route where traffic can easily be blocked.
An agreement to stop fighting for a time.
The government most countries and the U.N. officially accept as Yemen’s rulers.

stories.headline: Bosnia’s election hands wins to nationalists, and a pro-Russia leader thanks Trump
stories.dek: Banned from office, Serb separatist Milorad Dodik still claims victory as his allies sweep their region.
stories.caveman: Bosnia and Herzegovina is a small country in southeast Europe. In the 1990s, a brutal war between its three main groups — Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats — killed more than 100,000 people. A 1995 U.S.-brokered peace deal split power among the groups. It even has a three-person presidency: one Bosniak, one Serb, one Croat. On Sunday (Oct. 4) about 3.4 million people could vote. Nationalist parties — ones focused on their own ethnic group — gained across the board. Zeljka Cvijanovic, an ally of Serb leader Milorad Dodik, won more than 55% for the Serb seat, representing Republika Srpska, the Serb-majority half of the country. Dodik is banned from office and wasn’t on the ballot, but in his victory speech he thanked Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin.
stories.why_it_matters: Dodik wants the Serb region to break away and join Serbia. Stronger nationalists can mean more deadlock, slower progress toward joining the European Union, and a bigger foothold for Russia in Europe.
stories.camps: Dodik’s supporters say they are protecting Serb rights and self-rule. Analysts like Kurt Bassuener warn that every nationalist party gained, which threatens more instability, and that people may be voting out of fear rather than hope. Some ordinary voters told AP they want leaders of all groups to talk and compromise. Trump’s government lifted U.S. sanctions on Dodik last year; Biden’s team had imposed them over corruption and separatism.
stories.image_alt: Milorad Dodik holds up a ballot paper at a polling station in Laktasi, Bosnia

terms.explain: Putting your own nation or ethnic group first, sometimes against others.
Someone who wants a region to split off and become independent or join another country.
The Serb-majority half of Bosnia, with its own president and parliament.
A presidency shared by three people, one for each main ethnic group.
Bosnian Muslims, the largest ethnic group in Bosnia.

stories.headline: The Supreme Court’s new term opens with a climate fight — and guns, voting and deportations ahead
stories.dek: Can a Colorado town sue oil companies over climate damage? The justices heard that first.
stories.caveman: Every year the U.S. Supreme Court starts work on the first Monday of October. This year’s first day (Oct. 5) began with a big climate case. Boulder, Colorado, sued oil companies Suncor and ExxonMobil, saying they should help pay for damage linked to climate change. The companies, backed by the Trump administration, say a global problem shouldn’t be handled through local lawsuits. Later this term: whether states can ban AR-15-style rifles (December); Trump’s policy of deporting migrants to countries where they have no ties; holding immigrants without a bond hearing; Arizona rules requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote (December); and Catholic preschools left out of a Colorado program over rules about LGBTQ+ families (November).
stories.why_it_matters: The Supreme Court has the final word on what the Constitution means. Its decisions, usually announced by next summer, will shape climate lawsuits, gun laws, voting rules and immigration for years.
stories.camps: Climate groups and local governments say oil companies knew about climate risks and should share the costs. The companies and the administration say only Congress and federal agencies should set emissions policy. On guns, states with bans point to mass shootings, while challengers say AR-15s are common and protected by the Second Amendment. The court’s conservative majority has expanded gun rights in recent years.
stories.image_alt: The U.S. Supreme Court building in Washington at sunrise
stories.image_credit: Photo: J. David Ake/Getty Images via NBC News

terms.explain: The highest court in the U.S. Its nine justices decide what the Constitution and federal laws mean.
The court’s working year, which starts the first Monday in October.
The part of the U.S. Constitution about the right to “keep and bear arms.”
A court hearing where a judge decides if a detained person can be released while their case goes on.
To force a non-citizen to leave a country.

stories.headline: U.S. schools banned a record 12,000 books last year — and Stephen King tops the list again
stories.dek: PEN America’s new count lands during Banned Books Week; some districts now use AI to decide what to pull.
stories.caveman: PEN America is a group that defends free speech for writers. On Monday (Oct. 5), during Banned Books Week (Oct. 4–10), it released its yearly count: 11,982 cases of books being removed from U.S. public schools in the 2025–26 school year. That is the most since it started counting five years ago. The bans hit 7,370 different books; more than 4,500 were banned for the first time — from the classic “Jane Eyre” to the manga “Tokyo Ghoul.” Most bans happened in Texas and Florida, which passed strict laws. For the second year, Stephen King was the most-banned author (312 removals). The single most-banned book was Patricia McCormick’s “Sold,” about a girl trafficked into sexual slavery. Common reasons: race, sexuality and gender identity.
stories.why_it_matters: School libraries are where many kids first find books about lives unlike — or exactly like — their own. Who decides what stays on the shelf is a fight over parents’ rights, kids’ rights and free expression.
stories.camps: PEN and librarians say bans cut students off from diverse voices and that pulling books, even briefly, chills teachers. Supporters of removals, including many conservative parent groups and lawmakers, say they are protecting children from sexual or age-inappropriate content and that parents should have a say. Counts differ: the American Library Association, which only counts permanent removals, found about 5,600 bans in its latest report.
stories.image_alt: A Banned Books Week display with caution tape at a New York Public Library branch in the Bronx

terms.explain: A U.S. nonprofit of writers that defends free expression and tracks book bans.
An annual week each fall when libraries and bookstores highlight books that have been challenged or removed.
When a school or library removes a book or limits who can read it, often after complaints.
Japanese comic books, read by kids and adults around the world.
The main U.S. organization of librarians.

stories.headline: 42 years later, Stephen King finishes the “Talisman” saga he started with the late Peter Straub
stories.dek: “Other Worlds Than These,” the trilogy’s final book, out Oct. 6, is being called a moving goodbye to an old friend.
stories.caveman: In 1984, horror masters Stephen King and Peter Straub wrote “The Talisman,” about a 12-year-old boy, Jack Sawyer, who can “flip” between our world and a magical land called the Territories. A sequel, “Black House,” came in 2001. Straub sent King an idea for a third book back in 2013, but they never wrote it together; Straub died in 2022. Now King, 79, has finished it alone, and Straub’s name is still on the cover. In “Other Worlds Than These,” Jack is 57 and battered, trying to stop a death cult that wants to open a hungry black hole. The audiobook is read by comedian Patton Oswalt. Esquire’s critic says it will “break your heart.” It goes on sale Tuesday, Oct. 6.
stories.why_it_matters: It’s one of the biggest releases of the fall, from the most-banned author in U.S. schools — and a rare case of a writer finishing a story for a friend who has died.
stories.camps: Fans and critics like Esquire’s Anthony Breznican call it an emotional, page-turning adventure about aging and loss. Others are cooler: Kirkus found it entertaining but not either author at his best, and some reviewers say it leans so heavily on King’s “Dark Tower” books that newcomers may feel lost.
stories.image_alt: Publisher image pairing a photo of the two authors with the cover of “Other Worlds Than These”

terms.explain: A set of three connected books.
A book that continues the story of an earlier book.
A recording of a book read aloud.
Stephen King’s big fantasy series about a gunslinger, which connects to many of his other books.
Kirkus Reviews, a U.S. magazine that reviews books before they come out.

stories.headline: Ayad Akhtar’s new novel “The Radiance” takes on #MeToo, campus politics and Gen Z
stories.dek: The Pulitzer winner’s follow-up to “Homeland Elegies” is provocative — and already dividing critics.
stories.caveman: Ayad Akhtar is an American writer, born to Pakistani-born doctors. He won the 2013 Pulitzer Prize for Drama for his play “Disgraced,” and his novel “Homeland Elegies” was a big hit in 2020. His new novel, “The Radiance,” is set during COVID in a small upstate New York town. The narrator — also named Ayad, in a style called autofiction — is knocked off his bike by a hit-and-run driver. Afterward, he feels strangely calm and sees beauty everywhere. He starts teaching a writing class at a local college, and things go wrong: his prompts lead to sexual stories, including one hinting that a student was groomed by a professor friend. The book wrestles with #MeToo, short attention spans, online misinformation and trauma passed down in families.
stories.why_it_matters: Akhtar writes about the cracks in American life — race, religion, money, power. Novels like this become part of the national argument about free speech on campus and how we judge past relationships.
stories.camps: NPR’s Heller McAlpin calls it thought-provoking and finally “a profound reading experience,” though sometimes a head-scratcher. Vulture’s review headline — “Gen Z Gets a Drubbing” — signals that some readers will see its take on young people as unfair or grumpy. Akhtar’s fans say his job is to provoke; critics say provocation is not the same as insight.
stories.image_alt: Cover of “The Radiance” by Ayad Akhtar, with autumn trees

terms.explain: A top U.S. award for journalism, books, drama and music.

stories.headline: Billionaire MacKenzie Scott self-published a dystopian novel on Substack. The New Yorker isn’t impressed
stories.dek: “Last Days in Two Nations” imagines an America split in two — and critics are asking why she skipped a publisher.
stories.caveman: MacKenzie Scott is one of the richest women in the world and the ex-wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos. She is famous for giving away billions of dollars. Before that, she was a novelist: her first book won an American Book Award, and Toni Morrison was her teacher at Princeton. Since August, Scott has been posting her third novel, “Last Days in Two Nations,” serialized chapter by chapter for free on Substack, a newsletter website. It imagines a future America split into two countries; one, run by a germ-obsessed dictator-president, tests children for “rebelliousness.” The story jumps among 18 characters. In a New Yorker essay (Oct. 5), critic Rhoda Feng says it reads like a rushed draft or a movie script, with typos and clichés.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how much Amazon and self-publishing have changed books: even a famous literary writer now skips the big publishers. And the story’s obvious jabs at a real-life leader are part of a wave of political fiction in Trump’s second term.
stories.camps: Some see the free, self-published route as a quiet protest against her ex-husband’s company and the publishing gatekeepers. Others note that only a billionaire can afford that risk. Critics at The New Yorker and Vanity Fair say the book needed an editor; readers who like fast political thrillers may simply enjoy the ride.

stories.headline: “Defend our men!” Four Latin American countries push to punish false rape reports
stories.dek: Women’s groups say the bills in Bolivia, Chile, Argentina and Peru will scare real victims into silence.
stories.caveman: In Bolivia, Chile, Argentina and Peru, lawmakers have proposed laws to punish people who make false reports of domestic, sexual or gender-based violence — with prison terms of up to six years in some bills. Chilean senator Vanessa Kaiser, who backs one, says men must be defended from “horrible ideologies called feminism.” But the numbers show false reports are rare: in Argentina, about 1 in 1,000 criminal cases; in Bolivia, 0.13% of cases filed in 2024. Lying to police is already a crime in all four countries. The bigger problem, researchers say, is silence: in a 2024 Chilean survey, only 12.1% of women who suffered sexual violence reported it. In Argentina, only 15% of women killed in femicides in 2025 had reported abuse first.
stories.why_it_matters: Latin America’s women’s movements, like Ni Una Menos (“Not One Less”), won big changes in the last decade. These bills are part of a backlash. If victims fear jail for not “winning” their case, fewer will come forward.
stories.camps: Supporters say the bills protect the presumption of innocence and people wrongly accused of terrible crimes. Women’s rights groups and a regional treaty-monitoring body, MESECVI, say the bills look coordinated across countries and could create a new barrier to justice. Feminist lawyers in Argentina link them to President Javier Milei’s government closing women’s protection offices.
stories.image_alt: A protester with painted hand prints on her face at a Not One Less march in Buenos Aires
stories.image_credit: Photo: Luis Robayo/AFP/Getty Images via The Guardian

stories.headline: Women journalists accuse Delhi police of groping them at a youth protest over voter lists
stories.dek: India’s “Cockroach” protesters want the election chief out after 130 million names were cut from voter rolls.
stories.caveman: India’s Election Commission has been “cleaning” its voter lists for the first time in nearly 25 years. So far it has removed 130 million names, saying they were dead people, people who moved, or duplicates. Critics say the cuts could help Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s party, the BJP; the BJP and the commission deny that. Young protesters, many linked to the satirical online movement “Cockroach Janta Party,” gathered in Delhi and Mumbai for a third day on Sunday (Oct. 4), demanding that chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign. Police detained scores. Three women journalists say police officers touched them inappropriately. One student activist said police “dragged me by my hair.” Delhi Police say an inquiry has begun.
stories.why_it_matters: India is the world’s biggest democracy. Who gets to stay on the voter list decides elections. And whether reporters — especially women — can cover protests safely is a basic test of press freedom.
stories.camps: The Election Commission says the update is overdue and the lists are full of mistakes. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi says women fear for their safety and the government must “answer for this.” The Press Club of India demanded immediate action. Reports that two of Kumar’s fellow commissioners objected at least 14 times to decisions made without them fueled the protests; the commission says all decisions were unanimous.

stories.headline: An air strike on clearly marked U.N. food trucks kills a driver in Sudan
stories.dek: The attack in South Kordofan shows how dangerous it has become to feed 19.5 million hungry people.
stories.caveman: Sudan has been in a civil war since April 2023 between the army (SAF) and a paramilitary group called the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). On Saturday (Oct. 3), two trucks carrying food for the U.N.’s World Food Programme were hit from the air in South Kordofan state, while driving between two army-held cities. One driver was killed. WFP said the trucks were “clearly marked as humanitarian vehicles.” It did not name who did it and asked for an investigation; a Sudanese doctors’ group blamed RSF drones. Both sides use drones more and more. The war has forced 14 million people from their homes and killed tens of thousands.
stories.why_it_matters: About 41% of Sudan’s people faced severe hunger earlier this year, and 135,000 were at risk of famine. When aid trucks get bombed, food stops moving — and the people who need it most go without.
stories.camps: Aid agencies say attacks on aid workers break international law and demand that both sides let food through safely. Each armed side usually blames the other. On Monday, a U.S. envoy held a rare meeting with Sudan’s army chief, Gen. Abdel Fattah Burhan, to push for an end to the fighting — but past peace efforts have collapsed.

stories.headline: UK Conservatives pledge to cut foreign aid by 90% to pay for prisons; charities warn of damage
stories.dek: Kemi Badenoch would shrink aid from £9 billion to £1 billion a year, copying Reform UK’s plan.
stories.caveman: The UK gives money every year to help poor countries — for vaccines, disaster relief, fighting diseases like AIDS and malaria, and more. At the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham, party leader Kemi Badenoch said that if she becomes prime minister she will cut the aid budget from £9 billion a year to £1 billion, using the savings to help build 50,000 new prison places. The culture budget would also be cut by £1 billion a year. Charities and insiders say £1 billion would not even cover the UK’s existing promises to the U.N., the World Bank, the Gavi vaccine alliance and the Global Fund — those already add up to more than £1.6 billion a year.
stories.why_it_matters: Aid pays for things like children’s vaccines and emergency help after floods. Rich countries — the U.S. too — are cutting aid at the same time, so the world’s poorest people feel it twice.
stories.camps: Conservatives say British taxpayers’ money should go to problems at home first, like overcrowded prisons. Reform UK, which proposed the same £1 billion cap, agrees. Labour has already cut aid to 0.3% of the economy by 2027. Aid charities like Bond say the plan would wreck the UK’s global reputation and influence; the Liberal Democrats called it “un-British, unpatriotic and unwise.”
